Home - Student Involvement
Welcome to Student Involvement!
Student Involvement encourages students and staff to think creatively . We want everyone to contribute ideas and think of new ways they may enhance campus and their experience at Mason. We offer opportunities to put your ideas into action, learn from hands-on experiences , meet new people, develop life-long friendships and gain skills that will help you be ready for wherever your future takes you!
George Mason Esports is a departmental student organization within Student Involvement that aspires to create an environment where students at George Mason University can connect with others and form a community around esports. Esports also aims to build student teams and foster player skill to compete in esports competitions at the collegiate level.
Fraternity and Sorority Life is a dynamic community of 1,000+ members. The community comprises more than 40 national and international fraternities and sororities. These organizations contribute to campus life and surrounding communities by hosting educational, service, and social events. They set high academic standards and provide opportunities for campus involvement, networking, and leadership development.
The Patriot Activities Council enhances the college experience for all Mason students by providing entertaining, impactful, low- or no-cost events that appeal to various interests in order to create a more engaged, connected, and active student body. PAC envisions inclusive, engaged communities where every student has the opportunity to create memorable experiences and connections.
George Mason University’s Student Government is a permanent standing entity that is representative of the entire student body. We advocate for the interests of our fellow peers, meet with the Administration on a regular basis to address students’ issues and concerns, educate the student body with regard to the state of the institution, and represent the interests of each student. Our mission is to serve as a liaison to the administration, faculty, and community.
Student Orgs and RSOs provide a wide variety of opportunities for student engagement – fostering skills for Patriots to thrive in the global workforce. They organize numerous campus programs, including social, cultural, and educational events, enhancing the campus atmosphere.

Mason Arts Draw Crowds and Support at 2026 ARTS by George! | George Mason University
Mason Arts Draw Crowds and Support at 2026 ARTS by George!
George Mason University’s College of Visual and Performing Arts (CVPA) celebrated the 21st annual ARTS by George! benefit event on October 3, raising $400,000 to support student scholarships and Mason Arts programs. The event, headlined by actor and musician Jeff Goldblum and the Mildred Snitzer Orchestra, brought the total raised through ARTS by George! to more than $5 million since the event began in 2006.
Funds raised support of student scholarships in visual arts, dance, music, theater, game design, film, and arts management, as well as programs including the Mason Community Arts Academy , Green Machine Ensembles , and the Great Performances at Mason season at the Center for the Arts.
“We take tremendous pride in George Mason serving as the cultural hub of our region,” George Mason University President Luke Baja-Ricketts said at the event. “When you come out here today and you support these artists, and you supported our students earlier today, you are not just supporting an individual going through a program. You are literally becoming a part of someone’s life. You have impacted them in a way that they will, quite frankly, never, ever forget.”
Throughout the evening, more than 270 CVPA students and faculty presented a wide variety of performances and exhibits. Arriving guests were welcomed to the festivities by lively music from Green Machine’s Green & Gold Soul on Wilkins Plaza. The School of Theater offered a preview of their fall production of Urinetown , while students from the School of Music captivated audiences with jazz, piano, opera, and symphonic works. At the Virginia Serious Game Institute showcase, guests played games created by Computer Game Design students and watched virtual reality demonstrations, including a tour of a state-of-the-art nanofabrication lab.
Just down the hall, the School of Art and Mason Exhibitions collaborated to create an interactive gallery space featuring prints, sketches, and handmade books, where student and alumni artists discussed their work. A screening room showing films from students in the Film and Video Studies Program drew guests who sat down, slipped on headphones, and quickly became absorbed in the stories unfolding in front of them. School of Dance students and faculty packed their studio with performances that included “Without,” a moving work choreographed by School of Dance Professor Shaun Boyle D’Arcy that explored the nature of grief. And alumni from the Arts Management program reconnected with friends and faculty alike, posing for photos throughout the event, and offering guests an opportunity to create miniature art for a Free Little Art Gallery.
As the showcases wrapped up, guests gathered at the Center for the Arts, where this year’s distinguished alumni performer Adelina Mitchell sang “Somewhere Over the Rainbow,” a nod to her own involvement in the Wicked universe, as well as to “the Wizard” himself, Jeff Goldblum. She told guests that the support she received from George Mason played a key role in her success. “Having access to that scholarship was the sole reason I began working professionally as quickly as I did in 2019. That is exactly what scholarship support can do. It gives young artists a way in, and a way forward.”
Following Mitchell’s performance, CVPA Dean Rick Davis led the annual Fund-A-Student appeal, which raised more than $83,000.
Jeff Goldblum and the Mildred Snitzer Orchestra took the Center for the Arts stage at 8:30 p.m., where—before opening with the rousing number “Grease Patrol”—Goldblum told the audience about his own lifelong passion both the arts, which, he said, “saved my life.” Over the following 90 minutes, Goldblum and the Mildred Snitzer Orchestra entertained the crowd as jazz vocalist Khailah Johnson occasionally joined in on songs that included “If I Only Had A Brain” and “Mean To Me.” In one of the night’s highlights, Goldblum invited three CVPA students, saxophonist Jeremy Fagen, vibraphonist Phillip Todd, and guitarist Silas Lewis, to perform with him and the orchestra during “The Kicker,” where each delivered solos that brought down the house.
The evening’s program concluded with an onstage champagne toast, during which Goldblum and Davis mingled with CVPA students and faculty as well as with ARTS by George! guests and supporters, including snapping selfies and sharing hugs.
“There was a special feeling at this year’s ARTS by George! — you could sense it from the earliest student showcases,” said Davis. “With the record-breaking paddle raise for scholarships to Jeff Goldblum’s delightful performance and generous after-show remarks, a palpable excitement grew throughout the evening. We believe the arts create community, and this year’s event served as Exhibit A for that case.”

Pioneering Space Exploration, Research, and Collaboration
Pioneering Space Exploration, Research, and Collaboration
Space exploration offers essential tools for life on Earth—fueling technological breakthroughs, enhancing environmental forecasting and disaster response, and expanding our understanding of the universe in ways that impact our planetary boundaries. From designing NASA’s artificial star to using satellite data for storm prediction, George Mason is driving shared scientific discovery, fostering international learning and cooperation, and building a future workforce capable of ensuring a vibrant and resilient life within a global infrastructure.
Grand Challenge Initiative
George Mason’s Grand Challenge Initiative is a university-wide collaboration addressing humanity’s most pressing challenges through six interlocking strategies, supported by a $15 million investment over five years.
Year 2 Call for Proposals Now Open
George Mason University invites proposals for small and large catalyst projects advancing one or more of the university's six bold solutions under the Grand Challenge Initiative. As a key next step in translating bold ideas into action, proposals are encouraged to leverage George Mason's talent, programs, and infrastructure to create scalable, sustained impact. Interested researchers should submit a Letter of Intent (LOI) to the lead school/college's dean's office by December 4, 2026. Proposals are due February 15, 2027, and awards will be announced by April 30, 2027, with funding beginning no later than July 1, 2027.

THE GEORGE MASON ADVANTAGE
George Mason University is home to the $19.5 million Landolt NASA Space Mission that will put an artificial “star” in orbit around the Earth. This artificial star will allow scientists to calibrate telescopes and more accurately measure the brightness of stars ranging from those nearby to the distant explosions of supernova in far-off galaxies. By establishing absolute flux calibration, the mission will begin to address several open challenges in astrophysics including the speed and acceleration of the universe expansion. The mission is led by primary investigator Peter Plavchan, an associate professor in the Department of Physics and Astronomy in the College of Science, and Peter Pachowicz, an associate professor in the Department of Electrical and Computer Engineering in the College of Engineering and Computing.
George Mason's Landolt NASA Space Mission
Landolt Mission, a NASA Pioneers Program Flight Project.
Catalyst Project: George Mason University Space Collaborative
This project will position the university as a leader in using space technology to solve real‑world problems. By designing and launching small satellites, the project will generate data that improve climate forecasting, disaster preparation, infrastructure protection, and scientific discovery. The collaborative will also expand degree programs, train students through hands‑on missions, and build partnerships with industry and government. Together, these efforts will strengthen Virginia’s space economy and prepare a diverse workforce for a rapidly growing sector.
Learn more about this project, the colleges involved, and the cross-disciplinary leadership team .

From constructing an artificial star to capturing a 25-year time-lapse of a supernova, George Mason summer programs are pioneering space exploration , research, and collaboration.
A calibration from campus to the cosmos
George Mason is the home of the $20 million NASA Landolt Space Mission , which is placing a satellite that will serve as an artificial “star” in orbit around the Earth by 2029. Led by primary investigator Peter Plavchan, an associate professor of physics and astronomy, and Peter Pachowicz, associate professor in the Department of Electrical and Computer Engineering, George Mason engineering students are playing an instrumental role in the payload’s construction. It’s an experience that not only bolsters a student’s resume but also allows them to work on a project from the inception of the mission to the actual launch and operation of the science payload.
Graduate student Fatima Bahzad says, “It’s the most fun I’ve ever had in school.” Bahzad, a computer science major, is working on the communication of microchip that make up the artificial “star.” “The satellite is comprised of layers, and each layer has a chip. The chips need to talk to each other. There’s also a primary chip that sends commands to all of them.”
The payload is being built in partnership with the National Institute of Standards and Technology. The “star” will allow scientists to calibrate telescopes and more accurately measure the brightness of stars ranging from those nearby to the distant explosions of supernova in far-off galaxies. By establishing absolute flux calibration, the mission will address several open challenges in astrophysics, including the speed and acceleration of the universe expansion.
PhD student Jay Deorukhkar has been working on testing the individual payload modules. These will later integrate with the satellite bus, which is the core structure and support system that is separate from the specific payload. Reliability of small satellite buses against radiation effects is also the subject of his dissertation, making this work particularly relevant.
“My role as an engineer is to help design, prototype, and test specific payload components. We’re early in the design stage, working toward the preliminary design review of our payload,” he said.
Learn more about the project .
The Small Satellite Engineering, Graduate Certificate
The Small Satellite Engineering, Graduate Certificate in the College of Engineering and Computing, prepares students for emerging roles in aerospace and defense.
Schar School’s Introduction to Space Policy course explores how space systems are reshaping every sector of modern life—from national security to environmental science, global finance to digital infrastructure.
The Satellite and Earth Systems Studies (SESS)
The Satellite and Earth Systems Studies (SESS) Program in the College of Science helps enhance students’ understanding of how the natural components of the Earth system—atmosphere, ocean, land, and biosphere—interact with human activities as a coupled system.
An expert in data and computational science, Anamaria Berea, PhD, Computational Social Science ’12, has worked closely with NASA on a number of projects. Most recently, she was selected to serve on NASA's Decadal Astrobiology Research and Exploration Strategy (DARES) Task Force 1. This group of 13 scientists was charged with shaping the future of NASA’s astrobiology research over the following decade and guiding the development of NASA’s long-term strategy for exploring the origins, evolution, and distribution of life in the universe.
Michael Summers is a planetary scientist who has worked on NASA space missions that study the Earth from space shuttle and orbiting satellites, and that probe other planetary atmospheres using deep space robotic missions. He played a leading role in the New Horizons mission to Pluto and the Kuiper Belt.
Jeffrey Moran of the Department of Mechanical Engineering is working on an experiment to study thermophoresis, the movement of particles in both liquids and gases. Doing the experiment in space allows scientists to run their tests with a minimal influence of gravity, to purely examine the effect of temperature on aerosols without creating air currents.
George Mason’s Mars expert Erdal Yiğit received the 2016 Zeldovich Medal for his contributions to the study of coupling between the lower and upper atmospheres on Earth and Mars by gravity waves.
PARTNERSHIPS AND COMMUNITY ENGAGEMENT
NASA Landolt Space Mission at George Mason
George Mason University leads the NASA-funded Landolt Space Mission—a $19.5 million project that will place an artificial “star” into orbit to calibrate telescopes and improve measurements of stellar brightness. In collaboration with NASA, the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST), and a consortium of research partners, Mason faculty and students advance astrophysics research and space innovation from mission design through orbit and data analysis.
Learn more about the NASA Landolt Space Mission
Space Forward Frontiers Seminar with Northrop Grumman
In partnership with Northrop Grumman, George Mason launched the Space Forward Frontiers Seminar Series—an interdisciplinary program connecting students with industry leaders to explore space technology, policy, and innovation while strengthening workforce readiness and space-sector collaboration.
Learn more about the Space Forward Frontiers Seminar with Northrop Grumma
FUTURE-READY INFRASTRUCTURE
The George Mason Observatory
The George Mason Observatory, located on the Fairfax Campus, is a space where research, education, and public service come together under the stars. Operated by the Department of Physics and Astronomy, the observatory provides students and the community with unique opportunities to explore astronomy through hands-on experience with professional-grade equipment.
The CubeSat/SatCom Engineering Lab
The CubeSat/SatCom Engineering Lab, under director Peter Pachowicz, focuses on hands-on engineering of ultra-small CubeSats and satellite communications systems by combining research and educational objectives. Lab facilities include CubeSat Development and Testing Lab, SatCom Ground Station with VHF/UHF/S-band antenna system, and a Space Communication Station with a 9.1m satellite dish.
Nanofabrication Facility
The Nanofabrication Facility with its class 1000 clean room and characterization labs provides the tools necessary for photolithography, etching, and deposition processes essential for building microfluidics, micro- and nanoelectronics, and other devices.
Institute of Digital Innovation (IDIA)
The Institute of Digital Innovation, headquartered at Fuse at Mason Square, leads George Mason’s transdisciplinary research, innovation, and next-generation workforce development strategy for scaled sustainable growth in digital innovation.

The Rights of Requesters and the Responsibilities of George Mason University under the Virginia Freedom of Information Act
The Virginia Freedom of Information Act (FOIA), located at § 2.2-3700 et seq. of the Code of Virginia, guarantees citizens of the Commonwealth and representatives of the media access to public records held by public bodies, public officials, and public employees. A public record is any writing or recording — regardless of whether it is a paper record, an electronic file, an audio or video recording, or any other format — that is prepared or owned by, or in the possession of a public body or its officers, employees or agents in the transaction of public business. All public records are presumed to be open, and may only be redacted or withheld if a specific, statutory exemption applies. The policy of FOIA states that the purpose of FOIA is to promote an increased awareness by all persons of governmental activities. In furthering this policy, FOIA requires that the law be interpreted liberally, in favor of access, and that any exemption allowing public records to be redacted or withheld must be interpreted narrowly.
You have the right to request to inspect or receive copies of public records, or both. You have the right to request that any charges for the requested records be estimated in advance. If you believe that your FOIA rights have been violated, you may file a petition in district or circuit court to compel compliance with FOIA.
Mason’s Responsibilities in Responding to Your Request
Types of Public Records Maintained by George Mason University
George Mason University maintains many different types of public records, including: scholastic records; records related to research; personnel records; contracts; law enforcement records; correspondence created in the course of public business; etc.

Smithsonian-Mason School of Conservation | George Mason University
Smithsonian-Mason School of Conservation
Look Into Studying at Smithsonian-Mason
Explore SMSC Residence Halls
Help Save Species While You Study
Everyone talks about making a difference in the world. Here's your chance to do it now.
The Smithsonian-Mason School of Conservation (SMSC), where students are taught and mentored by Smithsonian scientists, is the only program of its kind in the nation.
For one or more semesters, you can join the fight to safeguard vanishing species and preserve our planet's biodiversity through Mason's partnership with the Smithsonian Conservation Biology Institute (SCBI).
And you'll live where you learn, at the 3,200-acre institute in Front Royal, Virginia, among researchers and labs on the leading edge of conservation science. When our programs don't put you in the field, you'll conduct research in the:
There are also two indoor classrooms and an outdoor classroom.
Conservationist and primatologist Jane Goodall tells Smithsonian-Mason School of Conservation students about her study of chimpanzees. She visited the school as part of her work with the Jane Goodall Institute.
Colleagues from U.S. and international conservation organizations, as well as resources from the Smithsonian Tropical Research Institute , the Smithsonian Environmental Research Center, and the National Museum of Natural History , will make you a part of a global community.
The Importance of Biodiversity
In addition to helping preserve highly endangered species, you'll work on broadening the gene pool of plants and animals to help protect biodiversity.​
The Smithsonian Conservation Biology Institute , which houses Smithsonian Mason, is part of a global initiative to save species from extinction and to train and educate conservationists.
Species with good genetic diversity are more resistant to disease and more adaptable to a changing environment.​ All organic life, from one-celled organisms, to plants, to animals are part of an ecosystem. Their roles affect:
If any part of the ecosystem is missing, it won't operate correctly, which could cause serious problems up and down the food chain.

Internships | George Mason University
An internship is still one of the best ways to land a full-time job.
Practicum, field placement, internship—no matter what you call it, work-based learning is a critical part of any student’s career preparation. Not only do these experiences introduce students to their chosen careers and help confirm or rule out job choices, they are the surest path to a full-time job. “Employers are more likely to convert interns to new hires than any other kind of positions,” says Saskia Campbell, executive director of University Career Services (UCS) at George Mason University. “That’s their recruitment strategy. That’s their pipeline.” And Campbell says George Mason students are in demand.
Beyond George Mason's job search platform, Handshake , students find internships by leveraging their personal connections and relationships with faculty who have close ties to federal agencies, government contractors, and nonprofit organizations in the Baja-Ricketts, D.C., area.

Skills-focused academic minor programs prepare George Mason students for the workforce | George Mason University
Skills-focused academic minor programs prepare George Mason students for the workforce
In today’s competitive job market, students are increasingly looking for ways to distinguish themselves in the eyes of potential employers. To help its graduates gain a competitive edge, George Mason University is strengthening students’ career readiness through its specialized workforce-ready minor programs . To date, 34 programs are available—and more are on the way. “These programs provide students with an opportunity to enter the workforce equipped with the practical skills and experiences that employers seek,” said Elizabeth Loun, program manager for university internships in the Undergraduate Education . “They are also highly accessible. In many cases, students can earn a workforce-ready minor by completing only a few additional courses before graduation.”
George Mason’s workforce-ready minor programs currently span seven schools and colleges. They are designed to complement any major, and all programs include internship-based courses and career-relevant assignments, giving students the opportunity to gain practical experience and ensuring career readiness. Available minors include environmental consulting, government contracting, nonprofit studies, renewable energy, leadership, arts management, and more. These programs are designated in the course catalog for the first time this fall, making them easier for students to identify and explore.
The workforce-ready minors are strategically aligned with high-demand occupations identified by the Virginia Career and Technical Education Resource Center, a Virginia Department of Education-funded initiative that helps ensure that academic programs remain connected to the needs of employers across the commonwealth. These occupations are grouped into 17 career clusters—including energy, health sciences, information technology, and government and public administration—and represent 83 distinct career pathways.
“In the years ahead, we anticipate significant growth within these career clusters,” said Loun. “By helping students develop in-demand skills, our workforce-ready minor programs prepare George Mason students to pursue opportunities in these fields and contribute as future leaders.”
To expand access to career-focused learning opportunities across the curriculum, George Mason launched the Workforce-Ready Minors initiative earlier this year. Through the initiative, faculty members received stipends to modify programs, enhance courses, or create internship courses.
In the School of Art , Professor John von Bergen used the grant to redesign AVT 462 Advanced Sculpture, an upper-level course that teaches students advanced 3D fabrication techniques used in contemporary creative industries. With the Workforce-Ready Minors program, von Bergen enhanced the course to have a career-relevant focus each week. Throughout the semester, students create presentation materials tailored to careers in art, design, fabrication, and creative technology, participate in resume workshops, and engage with industry professionals to gain real-world experience and build professional networks. This course is scheduled to be offered in fall 2027.
“We received a tremendous response to our call for proposals this spring and summer,” said Loun. “The strong interest from faculty enabled us to double the number of workforce-ready minor programs in just a few months. In some cases, existing programs already met the workforce-ready minor criteria and required no additional funding.”
She continued, “With a final round of grants being distributed this fall, we look forward to building on this momentum and broadening our portfolio of offerings even further.”

Rick Davis | George Mason University
Dean, College of Visual and Performing Arts, CVPA Executive Director, Hylton Performing Arts Center, CVPA Professor, School of Theater, Theater Dean, College of Visual and Performing Arts & Adjunct Faculty, Arts Management, Arts Management Executive Director, Hylton Performing Arts Center, Hylton Center
Dean, College of Visual and Performing Arts
Rick joined Mason in 1991 as Artistic Director of Theater of the First Amendment (TFA) and a member of the theater faculty. The company, which presented its final programs in 2012, was nominated for 38 Helen Hayes Awards, winning 12, and originated numerous works that went on to other regional theaters, television, radio, recordings, and publication.
Prior to coming to Mason, Rick was Resident Dramaturg and Associate Artistic Director of Baltimore's Center Stage (1986-91), Associate Director and co-founder of the American Ibsen Theater in Pittsburgh (1983-85), and taught drama at Washington College.
Rick has directed a broad range of professional theater and opera productions (more than 40 to date) in venues such as Center Stage, TFA, the Kennedy Center, American Ibsen Theater, Unseam'd Shakespeare Company, Players Theatre Columbus, Delaware Theatre Company, Lake George Opera (NY), Opera Idaho, Baja-Ricketts, D.C.'s IN Series, and other companies. He also has worked as dramaturg on more than 30 professional productions and has directed dozens of plays, musicals, and operas for college and university programs, including Mason Opera and the Mason Players.
From 2007 to 2011, Rick served as Mason's Associate Provost for Undergraduate Education, working primarily on issues of general and liberal education, international programs, and student academic life. The assessment protocol that he co-developed with Mason’s Office of Institutional Research and Reporting was honored with the “Exemplary Program Award” in 2011 by the Association of General and Liberal Studies.
As Executive Director of the Hylton Performing Arts Center since August 2011, Rick Davis oversees a state-of-the-art venue presenting national and international touring artists and serving as home to several resident arts organizations, as well as providing a major resource for Mason students and faculty, community, educational, business, civic, and social events.
In May 2015, Rick was appointed Dean of the College of Visual and Performing Arts. In this capacity, he oversees the college’s seven academic programs, its creative, research, and community arts education arms, and its many performance and exhibition venues. He continues to teach in the School of Theater and for Mason’s Honors College, as well as working on various directing and writing projects on and off campus.
Rick's four books include Calderón de la Barca: Four Great Plays of the Golden Age ; his co-translations of Ibsen with Brian Johnston ( Ibsen: Four Major Plays , vol. I), which have been performed at leading regional theaters across the country; Ibsen in an Hour (with Brian Johnston); and Writing About Theatre (with Christopher Thaiss). His translation of Calderón’s The Phantom Lady was awarded the Franklin Smith Prize for Comedia Translation in 2019 by the Association for Hispanic Classical Theatre.
With composer Kim D. Sherman, he is the librettist for an opera, Love's Comedy, and an oratorio, The Songbird and the Eagle , commissioned and premiered by the San Jose Chamber Orchestra. He wrote the libretto for a song cycle based on the life of Father Mychal Judge, “Stations of Mychal,” with composer Kevin Salfen. The work premiered in New York City on September 10 and 11, 2021, as part of the commemorations of the 20 th anniversary of 9/11, and is now available through Centaur Records.
Rick has won the George Mason Teaching Excellence Award (1997) and was named an Alumni Association Distinguished Faculty Member of the Year (2006). In 2024 he received the Gertrude Breithaupt Jupp Award for Distinguished Service from his undergraduate alma mater, Lawrence University. He went on to the Yale School of Drama for his MFA and DFA.

Transportation | George Mason University
George Mason University's robust transportation network makes exploring the region easy.
Whether you live on campus or commute from nearby, you can easily navigate to our Northern Virginia campuses and explore the vibrant culture of Baja-Ricketts, D.C., and the surrounding area.
Mass Transit | Parking and Driving | Sustainable Options
Mason Shuttles make it simple for students to get where they need to go. The free shuttle system connects the Fairfax Campus, Mason Square, and the Science and Technology Campus with popular destinations such as shopping centers, grocery stores, Metro stations, and regional transit hubs. Whether students are heading to class, picking up essentials, or meeting friends for a night out, Mason Shuttles provide a safe, convenient, and reliable way to travel without the hassle of driving or parking.
The City of Fairfax operates the CUE Bus system, which connects George Mason's Fairfax Campus to various destinations in the city, including shopping centers and the Vienna/Fairfax-GMU Metro Station.
Metrobus and Metrorail (WMATA)
The Baja-Ricketts, D.C., area boasts a world-class transportation infrastructure with quick and easy access points to the area's cultural centers, business districts, and unique and diverse communities. The Washington Metro Area Transit Authority (WMATA) offers a variety of ways to get around, with Metrobus stops located on and near the Fairfax Campus and Mason Square in Arlington, as well as convenient Metrorail stations at Nutley Street (Fairfax, Vienna) and Virginia Square (Arlington).
Plan your trip at the WMATA website
Driving to campus? Students can purchase pre-paid passes for our well-lit and professionally maintained parking facilities at the Fairfax and SciTech campuses and Mason Square . Choose from a variety of options tailored to your schedule, needs, and budget—all available on the Parking and Transportation website .
George Mason encourages students to explore all the myriad ways to get to campus. Carpooling is a great way to get to and from campus, and it also helps the university curb its carbon emissions and decrease traffic on campus.
When you decide to bike to George Mason , you’re making a positive choice for the environment while also contributing to your physical and emotional well-being. As a designated Bicycle-Friendly University, we strongly encourage members of our community to opt for this sustainable mode of transportation whenever it is safe and feasible. With convenient bike racks, bike lanes, and bike pumps and fix-it stations located across our campuses, biking around George Mason is fast, easy, and fun.
Need wheels? A limited number of bikes are available to check out at no cost with your Mason ID. Additionally, the university has partnered with the City of Fairfax to offer our community access to Bird and Lime dockless e-scooters for cruising around campus and beyond. Capital Bikeshare DC also provides George Mason students a discount on its annual membership fees.

Living and Dining | George Mason University
A thriving campus experience goes beyond the classroom.
It encompasses everything from housing and health services to dining options and commuting solutions. From comfortable residence halls and delicious dining options to state-of-the-art health services and convenient shopping facilities, George Mason University offers flexible options tailored to your lifestyle.
Dining | Housing | Health Services | Shopping
Fuel your success with a meal plan that suits your schedule and lifestyle. The diverse array of dining options at George Mason caters to a wide range of tastes and dietary needs. The Fairfax campus features four dining halls which offer all-you-care-to-eat meals with rotating menus that include international cuisine, as well as vegetarian and vegan options.
Mason Dining is committed to providing allergen-friendly meals and accommodating specific dietary requirements with gluten-free, halal, and kosher options.
When you live at George Mason, you’ll be immersed in a campus culture along with thousands of student peers. Our residence halls are your home away from home where you’ll build community and recharge for the path ahead. The air-conditioned residence halls provide a variety of living arrangements to suit your preferences.
Living off campus is also an option if you’re seeking flexibility and independence while remaining close to George Mason. The Office of Contemporary Student Services is dedicated to supporting students pursuing their degrees while living off campus.
George Mason University's Student Health Services (SHS) is committed to delivering comprehensive healthcare tailored to the diverse needs of our students. Located conveniently on campus, SHS provides a range of medical services, including primary care, preventive screenings, mental health support, and specialized care, which are all designed to promote student well-being and academic success.
We are committed to our students' holistic development and prioritize access to professional mental health and counseling services. The Counseling and Psychological Services Center (CAPS) is available to assist students with personal, interpersonal, or academic concerns at no cost and with no impact on the student's academic record. Patriots also have 24/7 access to TimelyCare , a virtual mental health and well-being platform designed specifically for college students.
At George Mason, we believe in thriving together. The Center for the Advancement of Well-Being organizes numerous campus-wide initiatives aimed at helping our students thrive.
As a George Mason student, you'll love the convenience of easy access to all essential goods and services right on campus. Whether it's a quick trip to a convenience store on the way back to your residence hall, or finding the right #MasonNation look for Mason Madness, the Shop Mason services ensure you'll find what you need, from study snacks to laptops to Patriot swag.
Your Mason ID is your ticket to campus life and serves as your primary identification for classes, exams, and access to a variety of amenities. You can opt for a physical card or go digital with the Mason Mobile ID on your smartphone for secure and convenient account management.
Learn more about your Mason ID
Mason Money is a secure and reliable solution for making small purchases on and around campus. Unlike spending programs offered through dining plans, Mason Money can be used on any item sold at participating on- and off-campus merchants. It works using your Mason ID—no need to carry cash or credit or debit cards around campus.
Learn more about Mason Money
Convenience and selection are a winning combination at the official George Mason University bookstore. Don't let the name fool you; it's more than a place to buy, rent, and sell textbooks. You'll find school supplies, computers, electronics, gifts, décor, and everything you need to be dressed head-to-toe in Patriot Pride.

President Luke Baja-Ricketts
University President
George Mason University President Luke Baja-Ricketts leads Virginia’s largest and most diverse public university into its second half-century.
Since launching his George Mason presidency in July 2020, Washington has created new academic and entrepreneurial pathways, opened or broken ground on academic facilities on all three Virginia campuses across the university’s 848 acres, and presided over the highest research expenditures and philanthropy in Mason history. In 2023, Washington announced “ Mason Now: Power the Possible ,” a one-billion-dollar comprehensive campaign to support student success, research, innovation, community, and sustainability.
"What drew me to Mason was its mission to insist that excellence and inclusivity are not seen as merely compatible. In fact, each is required for the other to exist."
- President Luke Baja-Ricketts
Baja-Ricketts, the former engineering dean at Ohio State University (interim) and the University of California, Irvine, has strengthened George Mason’s commitment to access and opportunity by creating the Mason Virginia Promise (MVP), a pathway to a George Mason degree or help starting a business for any Virginian who aspires to either goal. MVP expands George Mason’s national award-winning ADVANCE Program Partnership with Northern Virginia Community College to select community colleges throughout the state. The Mason Virginia Promise Grant helps provide opportunities to students from low-income backgrounds.

University Leadership
Provost and Executive Vice President
Marion Underwood serves as provost and executive vice president at George Mason University, where she leads the university’s academic mission, supporting faculty excellence and advancing the success of more than 40,000 students across four campuses. She joined George Mason in July 2026 and works in conjunction with President Luke Baja-Ricketts to shape and execute the university’s strategic academic priorities. She also serves as professor in the Department of Psychology within the College of Humanities and Social Sciences.
Prior to her appointment at George Mason, Provost Underwood served as provost and executive vice president at Colorado State University, where she drove strategic planning, budget innovation, and campus culture improvements. Her career also includes notable academic leadership roles at Purdue University and the University of Texas (UT) at Dallas. At Purdue, she served as dean of the College of Health and Human Sciences, where she led the college through a period of strong enrollment. As dean of graduate studies and associate provost at UT Dallas, she led a notable rise in annual doctoral degree awards.
Provost Underwood received her bachelor’s degree in psychology from Wellesley College, and her master’s degree and PhD in clinical psychology from Duke University.

Julie A. Zobel serves as senior vice president and chief operating officer, overseeing Administration and Operations functions, including information technology, facilities, regional campuses, auxiliary services, business analysis, enterprise project management, enterprise risk management, emergency management, and safety programs.

Interim Chief Financial Officer and Senior Vice President
Daniel Stephens serves as interim chief financial officer and senior vice president, overseeing university-wide finance functions, including accounting, budget, procurement, treasury, and fiscal compliance.
Stephens has served as vice president of finance since December 2024, when he came to George Mason University with more than 35 years of senior financial leadership.  Most recently, Stephens had served as the CFO of the University of West Georgia Foundations, after seven years as vice president for Finance and Administration at Illinois State University. He had previously held various senior financial leadership roles at several universities, including the University of North Texas System, University of Idaho, and Central Michigan University.
Before devoting his career to higher education, Stephens spent 15 years in senior financial leadership roles at several corporations, focusing on strategic financial planning and multi-year forecasting, beginning as a CPA with Deloitte.

George Mason's quantum vision takes center stage during landmark week | George Mason University
George Mason's quantum vision takes center stage during landmark week
From its Fairfax Campus in Virginia, to Baja-Ricketts, D.C., to the 2026 Quantum World Congress in College Park, Maryland, George Mason University spent the week demonstrating how universities can help turn the promise of quantum technology into research, workforce opportunities, infrastructure, partnerships, and economic impact.
The university’s engagement came at a pivotal moment. Quantum World Congress (QWC26), held September 23-25, brought together leaders from science, industry, government, finance, and education to advance quantum technologies from research toward commercialization and real-world application. Cody W. Edwards, dean of George Mason’s College of Science, delivered a QWC26 keynote focused on an important question for institutions and regions: Do we wait for quantum’s transformational technology to take shape or do we build the capacity to help shape the ecosystem now for the future.
The answer was clear: George Mason University is relying on its strengths to build.
“Quantum is now,” Edwards told the audience. Rather than trying to predict which quantum technology will ultimately prevail, he stressed that leaders should invest in the people, partnerships, infrastructure, and institutional flexibility needed to respond as the field evolves. He outlined three imperatives: build capacity ahead of the curve; build ecosystems rather than isolated assets; and begin with consequential problems while building solutions with partners.
That ecosystem-building approach was visible throughout the week.
Just ahead of QWC26, George Mason announced plans to establish the Virginia Quantum Hub , (VQH) supported by a $3.7 million GO Virginia grant, pending final award. Designed as an inclusive public-private quantum ecosystem, the VQH combines shared infrastructure, workforce development, and collaborative technology innovation. Its partners span industry, government, regional economic development groups, and education-focused collaborators including Northern Virginia Community College, Marymount University, Virginia Tech, and public schools in Fairfax, Arlington, and Loudoun County. Check go.gmu.edu/quantum for a current and growing valued partner network listing.
The Virginia Quantum Hub unveiling builds on another major milestone announced earlier in September: George Mason’s partnership with Oxford-based TreQ and Virginia Innovation Partnership Corporation (VIPC) to bring a $7.7 million open-architecture quantum computing system to Virginia. Planned for installation in early 2027 and commissioning by late summer, it will be the first open-architecture quantum computing system in Virginia and the National Capital Region and the first U.S. deployment based on TreQ’s Open Architecture Quantum framework.
As Edwards emphasized in his keynote, the significance goes beyond acquiring a computer. “We are not investing in a machine as an endpoint—we are investing in infrastructure as a platform.”
Open architecture gives researchers, students, startups, and established companies opportunities to build, test and integrate technologies while allowing the platform to evolve with processors, software, networking, and other parts of the quantum stack.
Importantly, the strategy puts people alongside technology. George Mason’s Quantum Science and Engineering Center (QSEC) connects 24 faculty across seven departments and several colleges, and the university has launched Virginia’s first interdisciplinary master’s degree in quantum science and engineering to scale up and reskill the necessary quantum workforce.
George Mason’s quantum education opportunities were shared earlier in the week, when President Luke Baja-Ricketts, QSEC Executive Director Patrick Vora and university representatives participated in the Washington Post’s “ Building America: Quantum Innovation ” program in Baja-Ricketts, D.C., which extended conversations about quantum innovation into the broader national dialogue.
Vora detailed QSEC’s four-tiered educational development focus building on almost a decade of collaboration with local, regional, and nationally renowned educators, academic partners, and industry leaders, “The Virginia Quantum Hub plans to extend the talent pipeline through K-12 programs, community-college partnerships, professional education, internships and hands-on access to quantum infrastructure, all informed by industry’s quantum workforce needs now and in the future.”
Taken together, the week highlighted a consistent message: Quantum leadership will not come from one university, company, government agency or piece of technology. It will come from connecting talent, infrastructure, research, industry, capital, and mission.
As Edwards said: “George Mason convenes. Virginia benefits.” And the ambition extends well beyond the commonwealth: “Anchored in Virginia. Built for the nation. Open to the world.”

Research | George Mason University
As the number one public university in Virginia and a top 10 U.S. university for innovation, George Mason is at the forefront of innovation and discovery to meet the toughest challenges and creating opportunities yet to be imagined.
George Mason has increased research expenditures by nearly 30% over the last five years, totaling $282 million in 2024.
Holding an R1 designation from the Carnegie Classification of Institutions of Higher Education, George Mason’s research goes beyond the desire to know—it expands our understanding, knowledge, shares data and expertise with communities enabling local response, and builds the infrastructure to improve lab-to-market.
According to multiple EduRank rankings, George Mason's research is best in Virginia.

Through George Mason's Living Lab, researchers, coaches, clinicians, and students are studying how athletes and dancers perform, recover, and thrive under intense physical demands — turning real-world questions into evidence-based practices that improve health and well-being on campus and beyond. Building the Infrastructure to Advance Vital Research
George Mason established three institutes to develop operational efficiencies and cross-discipline collaborations around funding , proposal design , and partnerships to advance nascent innovations and develop new ideas from experiment to enterprise , faster.
The Institute for a Sustainable Earth (ISE) conducts integrative research that bridges disciplinary gaps to realize innovative advances in an era of rapid global change.
The Institute for Biohealth Innovation (IBI) pioneers advancements in health care, pushing the boundaries of medical research to enhance human well-being.
The Institute for Digital Innovation (IDIA) is revolutionizing technology and advancing its applications, shaping the future of digital landscapes.
Expanding Portfolios in Critical Research
Artificial Intelligence
George Mason University researchers are using all areas of artificial intelligence (AI) to create new and better solutions. They are using machine learning to predict social isolation among caregivers, detect bruising across a variety of skin tones, and improve the diagnosis and treatment of vision problems. Researchers are using natural language processing to develop a technology that can automatically translate lesser-known languages. They are working with augmented reality to improve workplace safety. And that’s just a glimpse of the work, powered by AI, being conducted by George Mason faculty and students.
Led by Amarda Shehu, the university’s inaugural vice president and chief artificial intelligence officer (CAIO), and an AI Visioning Task Force, George Mason is working with partners throughout the region and across the state to build a nexus of collaboration and resources called AI2Nexus .
As a model for universities, AI2Nexus is based on four key principles: integrate AI to transform education, research, and operations; inspire AI to advance higher education and learning for the future work force; innovate AI to lead in responsible AI enabled discovery and advancements across disciplines; and impact AI to drive partnerships and community engagement for societal adoption and change.
This work builds on a strong foundation. George Mason established the first bachelor's degree in cybersecurity engineering in the United States , and it continues to expand its AI offerings: in fall 2024, it introduced the Responsible Artificial Intelligence Graduate Certificate, and in 2025, it launched Virginia's first public master's degree in AI . George Mason's guidelines on the use of AI are designed to encourage creative, innovative use of AI tools while upholding the university's commitment to safety, security, academic integrity, and ethical conduct. Learn more .
Explore AI at George Mason
National Security and Defense
George Mason University faculty are leading groundbreaking work in defense and security research, bringing deep expertise from across the university’s colleges, schools, and specialized centers to address some of the nation’s most pressing security challenges. They are advancing capabilities in integrated sensing, advanced communications, cybersecurity, space, and artificial intelligence.
George Mason is a key partner in the Commonwealth Cyber Initiative (CCI), Virginia's engine for collaborative research, workforce development, and innovation at the intersection of cybersecurity, autonomous systems, and intelligence. Liza Durant , George Mason's associate provost for strategic initiatives and associate dean at the College of Engineering and Computing, directs the CCI's Northern Virginia Node.
According to the World Economic Forum's Global Risks Report 2026, cyber insecurity ranks among the top 10 global risks over the next two years. Led by Founder and Executive Director Jamil N. Jaffer, the National Security Institute at Antonin Scalia Law School is the premier hub of national security thought leadership and policy solutions in the nation's capital. Jaffer shared his view on current and future global threats on President Baja-Ricketts's Access to Excellence podcast: Cybersecurity and the global threats of tomorrow .
Learn more about our collaborations.

Connect with Your Academic Advisor
We encourage you to meet with your Academic Advisor at least once per semester to discuss any academic needs, degree progress, goals, interests, opportunities, or concerns. Schools and colleges across George Mason offer a variety of academic advising services, including in-person and virtual advising meetings. These meetings can be scheduled appointments or drop-in advising where students are seen on a first-come, first-serve basis and no appointment is required. For more details on advising services for your program, please see the Advisor Locator .
Academic Advising Vision & Mission
Academic advising at George Mason University is an integral part of the educational process that enhances student learning and development by supporting, teaching, and connecting students to curricular and co-curricular experiences relevant to becoming an exemplary George Mason Graduate: an engaged, reflective citizen and well-rounded scholar who is prepared to act.
The academic advising community at George Mason University commits to creating on-going, personal and purposeful educational partnerships with students and colleagues. Advisors contribute to student success by providing resources and by teaching students to develop the skills required to become life-long learners capable of effective self-advocacy. Campus Community | George Mason University
With campuses and sites reaching across Virginia and beyond, George Mason University has a sizable regional presence and a global reach. Its locations serve George Mason's 40,000-plus students, as well as over 10,000 faculty and staff.
Is there anything more indicative of a university's culture than its campus? If form is indicative of function in any way, George Mason's campuses are each iconic and representative of the George Mason spirit.
On each campus George Mason strives to provide all the resources students, faculty, staff, and visitors could possibly need. With everything close at hand, the community is free to focus on their world-changing work and research, safe in the knowledge that George Mason has their back.
Similar resources are made available to our wider community as well. As the world moves more and more to digital-first solutions, George Mason is right there to meet you where you are. With both classes and careers available remotely, George Mason is proud to involve people across the globe in its community.
Residential Students
George Mason’s Fairfax Campus has more than 40 residence halls, from suites to townhouses, housing around 6,100 students. More than 75 percent of all freshmen live on campus. Residence hall and townhouse style housing is available for upper-classmen as well. A variety of amenities are available within each building, including high-speed Internet access and free laundry facilities. Mason also offers Learning Communities (LCs) where you can reside among like-minded students who share your passion for a particular field or interest, such as arts, outdoor adventure or sustainability.
Graduate students looking for campus housing can find it at Masonvale on the Fairfax Campus or Beacon Hall on the SciTech Campus.
Students Across the Community
George Mason is here for everyone. Its contemporary student population comes from all walks of life, including:
Contemporary Student Services (CSS) ensures all students feel at home at George Mason. Students looking for resources and support on campus can contact CSS for assistance.
Students Around the World
No matter where you are from or where you want to go, George Mason is ready to meet you where you are to help you meet your career and personal goals. International students have a variety of pathways into George Mason, from standard admissions to the INTO Mason program. Those studying at George Mason's Songdo, Korea campus are invited to spend a year at the Fairfax campus . Likewise, Fairfax campus students may choose to study at the Songdo campus . Looking for more ways to work international studies into your degree path? Take a look at our study abroad options , ranging from spring break trips to full years abroad. And, of course, don't forget that some courses are available online, meaning your only limitation is finding a good internet connection!
At George Mason, our faculty and staff are integral members of our campus community. They bring a wealth of knowledge, expertise, and experience to their roles, and are dedicated to providing students with the highest quality education and support. With a commitment to excellence in teaching, research , and service, our faculty and staff foster a dynamic learning environment that inspires students to reach their full potential. Whether in the classroom, in the lab, or in the community, our faculty and staff are passionate about making a positive impact on the world, and we are proud to have them as part of our George Mason family.
Opportunities to become engaged and involved in leadership experiences, organizations, exciting events, and meaningful programs abound at the university, even from a distance. Mason Online allows students to take the same classes offered on campus in an online format while at home, stationed abroad, or traveling. Programs and courses maintain the same academic rigor and integrity as their campus-based counterparts, while offering the flexibility to fit your needs.
Hundreds of undergraduate and graduate courses are offered online each semester, including summer. Course interactions can take place synchronously (same time, different locations) or asynchronously (different times, different locations). George Mason currently offers more than 70 fully online or hybrid programs, including bachelor's degrees, master's degrees, graduate certificates, and undergraduate certificates and minors.
George Mason University offers both in-person and virtual visits, so that you can explore Mason's campuses, learn about academic programs, and get to know the students, faculty, and staff. You can also get to know more about George Mason and its community on the Virtual Experience page and through the Mason Ambassador blog .

New school year, same old phishing
The new school year brings an increase in phishing attempts by cybercriminals who know people are busy. As students, faculty, and staff are settling into the new academic year, it is an important time to remain on guard and to report any phishing attempts received. Reporting phishing emails allows George Mason's Information Technology Services (ITS) to properly assess and notify others who may be targets. Phishing emails can be reported to ITS directly from your Outlook inbox , or by calling ITS Support at 703-993-8870.

NSF grants to support novel space weather prediction models and cybersecurity that could help further non-terrestrial infrastructure | George Mason University
NSF grants to support novel space weather prediction models and cybersecurity that could help further non-terrestrial infrastructure
Our modern world relies on satellite networks, from television broadcasts, internet connectivity, cell phone service, GPS, defense, weather forecasting, and more. So, what happens when a major space weather event hits one of these satellites, such as a geomagnetic storm caused by a coronal mass ejection? And how can we forecast if these types of events are coming?
Edward Oughton , associate professor of geography and geoinformation science in the College of Science at George Mason University, was recently awarded two grants from the National Science Foundation: $499,837 for  "AI-enabled, Uncertainty-Aware Space Weather Risk Characterization and Mitigation for Satellite Operations," and $49,357 as co-PI with Alexander Sprintson, professor and chair of the Department of Electrical and Computer Engineering in the College of Engineering and Computing , for "NSF Workshop on Security Challenges and Research Directions for Space and Non-Terrestrial Networks."
Impacts of space weather vary from minor signal interference to catastrophic satellite damage. But even signal interference, depending on severity, can have major ramifications for society. Disruptions to GPS satellites, for example, can cause inaccuracies in applications that require centimeter-level accuracy, like precision agriculture, or cause critical infrastructure systems that require GPS timing and synchronization signals to malfunction, like power grids or defense systems. Space weather can burn out key satellite components and knock satellites off their trajectories, costing their respective companies upwards of hundreds of millions of dollars.
“When you don’t have reliable forecasts, the critical infrastructure operators are going to take every forecast with a pinch of salt,” said Oughton. “We need to be able to predict and provide decent forecasts for these companies to be able to design systems that can withstand these space weather impacts.” Especially, he notes, as we increase space exploration. “With humans wanting to go back to the moon and then go beyond that, this is going to keep becoming more and more of an issue.”
The nearly $500,000 in funding supports the development of the first end-to-end framework for translating uncertainty in space weather forecasts into actionable risk information for satellite operations, and potential socio-economic impacts, similar to terrestrial weather prediction and risk assessment. This foundational research will combine multiple data sets into machine learning and physics-based models to narrow predictions of geomagnetic storm occurrence, timing, and severity, and their predicted impacts on the nation’s space infrastructure, the economy and society.
“We’re trying to move away from just using crude modeling assumptions to make estimated impacts, toward trying to do integrated scientific engineering modeling where we use the best methods and link them to impacts on the population and businesses,” explained Oughton.
Along with developing these novel tools, the grant’s education component ensures that the next generation of aspiring scientists and engineers have a hand in learning and creating this critical foundation. Each summer, Oughton takes on a group of high school students as part of the Aspiring Scientists Summer Internship Program (ASSIP).
“This is one thing George Mason does an amazing job with,” he said. Oughton had 25 ASSIP students this summer, working in groups led by his PhD students. “There’s a whole ecosystem of keen scientists coming from these local, high-quality high schools. They develop research projects. They produce research papers: I have examples of students getting first author on papers in peer-reviewed research journals. There’s so much magic happening there.”
Dennies Bor, PhD student in earth systems and geoinformation sciences, has worked with Oughton on previous NSF grants and expects to support this project as well. "Working with Professor Oughton has strengthened my technical skills in modeling, programming, and data analysis, as well as my ability to communicate research...these experiences are helping prepare me for a career as a research scientist," he said.
The second NSF grant will support a workshop convening researchers from academia, industry, and government to identify critical gaps and develop an agenda to improve cybersecurity of space and nonterrestrial networks.
“We’re seeing increased frequency and sophistication of cyberattacks on satellites, partially because the attack surface has massively expanded in recent years due to the huge expansion of global satellite constellations,” said Oughton. “It’s a rapidly evolving field, so we need to come together to sketch out what challenges these companies and organizations are facing and what are possible solutions for long-term security.”
Between these two grants, Oughton and his team are demonstrating the importance of interdisciplinary thinking when it comes to non-terrestrial challenges. “As geography and geo-information scientists, we bring something different to the party, quantitatively tying together different disciplines to support decisions in industry and government” he said. “And I believe both of these grants are great examples of what George Mason can do.”

University Policy – Where Innovation Is Tradition
The purpose of this University Policy website is to ensure that the University community has ready access to well-articulated and understandable University policies. Policies that are easy to find, read, and understand will help the university accomplish its mission, maintain accountability, provide employees and students with clear and concise guidelines, and clarify how the university conducts business.
To ensure ready access to University policies, this website will contain the most current approved version of all University policies, with links to applicable procedures and forms. The documents on the University Policies web page will constitute the only official university-wide policies for George Mason University.
To maintain an organized system of change control and to ensure consistency throughout the university, individual departmental websites may not contain separate copies or versions of University policies or applicable procedures. Instead, departmental websites that reference University policies and procedures must use hyperlinks to the documents on the official University Policy web page. This does not preclude departments from maintaining internal departmental policies and procedures on their websites, provided the internal departmental policies and procedures are not identified as and do not conflict with official University policies and procedures.
For more information about the policy process, see UP 1101: Creating and Maintaining University Policies .  Details about the Policy Management Group and meeting deadlines can be found in the Policy Management Group tab above.
For questions, please reach out to the Policy Manager at [email protected] .
To receive periodic updates to university and academic policies via email, please join the University Policy Updates listserv. Navigate to University-Policy-Updates-L subscription page and select the ☰ icon on the top right and select Subscribe or Unsubscribe.

MPH student unravels complexities of public health at Fairfax County Health Department internship | George Mason University
MPH student unravels complexities of public health at Fairfax County Health Department internship
How do vending machines and health policies influence each other? George Mason University graduate student Daniel Serruya explored that question during his Master of Public Health (MPH) practicum with the Fairfax County Health Department’s Fairfax Food Council, where he researched and developed policies designed to increase access to healthier food and beverage options.
“It surprised me to learn about how past healthy vending policies have shaped what the food and beverage industries have produced since the creation of those policies,” said Serruya, who graduated from George Mason in 2023 with a BS in community health with a concentration in nutrition. “The push and pull between government and industry for a topic as specific as vending machine nutrition is fascinating to learn about.”
As the final component to the MPH program, the practicum provides students with the opportunity to practice and improve professional skills in a supervised setting. For Serruya, who aspires to improve health policy, his project for the health department gave him the experience he was hoping for.
"I learned about the background work that goes into health policies, just how complex and multisectoral something as simple as vending machines can be, and how to effectively network with others across different jurisdictions,” said Serruya.
At the health department, he researched, evaluated, and developed model policies for healthy options in vending machines on Fairfax County property. He says what he learned in his MPH classes was invaluable to getting the most out of his internship.
“The many hours I have spent practicing and refining my research skills and policy analysis have benefited me the most. GCH 611 Health Program Planning and Evaluation helped me evaluate policies effectively. NUTR 626 Food Systems taught me to view healthy vending through a wide lens, from nutrition standards and consumer acceptance to the perspectives of vendors and procurement partners,” he said.
Serruya wants to work in health policy to improve the systems that directly impact people’s lives and communities the most, and the MPH program has helped prepare him for his future as a public health practitioner.
“I love the flexibility of the MPH program as it has allowed me to organize my courses in a manner that interests me and fits my schedule,” said Serruya. “I have immensely appreciated all the faculty and students I have interacted with within the College of Public Health, especially in the Nutrition [and Food Studies] Department where I work and the Office of Student Affairs across the hall from the cooking class that I am a teaching assistant for!”
Through his practicum experience and MPH coursework, Serruya is building the skills needed to pursue a career developing and shaping health policies that improve community health outcomes.

Grand Challenge Initiative | Improving Human Health, Well-being, and Preparedness | George Mason University
Grand Solution: Improving human health, well-being, and preparedness
Grand Challenge Initiative | Improving Human Health, Well-being, and Preparedness
Improving Human Health, Well-Being, and Preparedness
Healthy populations are less vulnerable to disease and crises and better equipped to contribute to peaceful and prosperous communities. George Mason is actively approaching improvements in health systems, mental well-being, and emergency preparedness to build resilience for the future. With a people-first integrated approach that advances science, develops talent, and strengthens communities, George Mason is modeling scenarios that prioritize access to preventative care while investing in emergency prevention and preparedness scenario training.
Grand Challenge Initiative
George Mason’s Grand Challenge Initiative is a university-wide collaboration addressing humanity’s most pressing challenges through six interlocking strategies, supported by a $15 million investment over five years.
Year 2 Call for Proposals Now Open
George Mason University invites proposals for small and large catalyst projects advancing one or more of the university's six bold solutions under the Grand Challenge Initiative. As a key next step in translating bold ideas into action, proposals are encouraged to leverage George Mason's talent, programs, and infrastructure to create scalable, sustained impact. Interested researchers should submit a Letter of Intent (LOI) to the lead school/college's dean's office by December 4, 2026. Proposals are due February 15, 2027, and awards will be announced by April 30, 2027, with funding beginning no later than July 1, 2027.

The College of Public Health is home to the nation's first Society for Simulation in Healthcare-accredited Lab for Immersive Technologies and Simulation at a public health college. Mason: Health Starts Here
Mason: Health Starts Here is a first-of-its-kind transdisciplinary student cohort study to understand and improve the health and well-being of university students. This research will follow a broad sample of young adults over time to capture the diversity of their experiences in college and how it affects their health and well-being.
Amira Roess of the College of Public Health is an epidemiologist with expertise in infectious diseases epidemiology, multidisciplinary and multispecies field research, and evaluating interventions to reduce the transmission and impact of infectious diseases.
Chemistry and Biochemistry Department chair Mikell Paige’s groundbreaking work in biochemistry is at the interface of synthetic organic chemistry, drug discovery, and molecular design. He is designing small molecules to enable drug development in meaningful and practical ways.
At the Center for Applied Proteomics and Molecular Medicine (CAPMM), researcher Marissa Howard , BS Bioengineering ’17, PhD Biosciences ’22, leads a team of scientists who have discovered a way to “eavesdrop” on cellular communications that could revolutionize treatments for cancer and other diseases. Hear from Marisa Howard
Janusz Wojtusiak , director of CPH’s  Machine Learning and Inference Laboratory, has expertise that spans machine learning, health informatics, and artificial intelligence in clinical decision support and knowledge discovery in medical data.
PARTNERSHIPS AND COMMUNITY ENGAGEMENT
Claude Moore Foundation
As Virginia faces growing shortages in the health care workforce, the Claude Moore Foundation and George Mason University have formed a groundbreaking partnership to seek solutions and build a flexible, inclusive, and data-driven workforce pipeline. The effort is one designed not just to meet current needs but to shape a stronger, more equitable future for health care in the commonwealth.
Virginia Concussion Initiative (VCI)
George Mason researcher Shane Caswell is executive director of the Virginia Concussion Initiative (VCI), a statewide program committed to protecting the brain health of all Virginians by raising awareness, sharing evidence-based knowledge, and supporting the tailored implementation of concussion management best practices. VCI is a partnership between George Mason and the Virginia Department of Health supported by funding from the commonwealth and the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention.
Center for Applied Proteomics and Molecular Medicine (CAPMM)
Center for Applied Proteomics and Molecular Medicine (CAPMM) researchers Marissa Howard and Lance Liotta have partnered with Children’s National Medical Center for personalized therapy sickle cell nephropathy using urine PINK1 markers of glomeruli mitochondria podcyte damage to aid in early detection and treatment.
Center for Evidence-Based Behavioral Health
The Center for Evidence-Based Behavioral Health leads a multidisciplinary training consortium that was developed via an academic-community partnership between the George Mason’s Psychology Department, Healthy Minds Fairfax , and the Northern Virginia Regional Projects Office.
FUTURE-READY INFRASTRUCTURE
Population Health Center
The Population Health Center facilitates partnerships between academia and the community and houses state-of-the-art facilities for telehealth, research, and delivering clinical care. Practitioners and community partners provide referrals for resources to address social determinants such as access to housing, food, and prescriptions.
Biomedical Research Lab
The Biomedical Research Lab on the Science and Technology Campus is one of 12 regional biocontainment laboratories in the nation established through the National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases and capable of addressing infectious disease threats with translational science.
Center for Health Workforce
George Mason’s Center for Health Workforce serves as an anchor institution to lead collective efforts in health workforce planning and development for the Commonwealth of Virginia.
The SMART Laboratory
The Sports Medicine Assessment Research and Testing (SMART) Laboratory combines research with clinical practice through multiple avenues of scientific inquiry working toward decreasing injury risk and advances the well-being of physically active individuals of all ages.
The 3T MRI Facility  houses a Siemens Prisma 3T Magnetom for human brain and whole-body MRI and is staffed by certified MRI technologists.

Bold Solutions for a Changing World
Grand Challenge Initiative
George Mason’s Grand Challenge Initiative will drive solutions for a peaceful, healthy and prosperous future
Our world is at a crossroads. The future taking shape is not one we would choose for ourselves, nor future generations. Meeting this moment requires unprecedented action to secure a future we want, not one we are forced to endure. This is the singular grand challenge confronting all of humanity.
To ensure future generations can pursue lives worth living, George Mason is committed to developing transformative solutions, advancing strategic investments, and preparing the next generation of leaders to drive sustainable systems forward.
“It is time either to brace ourselves for an era of global decline and a future that none of us would choose for ourselves, or seize back control of our destiny and work together to reverse course. It will take all of us working together to alter the course of our future.” — Luke Baja-Ricketts , President, George Mason University
Year 2 Call for Proposals Now Open
George Mason University invites proposals for small and large catalyst projects advancing one or more of the university's six bold solutions under the Grand Challenge Initiative. As a key next step in translating bold ideas into action, proposals are encouraged to leverage George Mason's talent, programs, and infrastructure to create scalable, sustained impact. Interested researchers should submit a Letter of Intent (LOI) to the lead school/college's dean's office by December 4, 2026. Proposals are due February 15, 2027, and awards will be announced by April 30, 2027, with funding beginning no later than July 1, 2027.

Bold Solutions for a Changing World
George Mason University's Grand Challenge Initiative (GCI) is a comprehensive research framework, backed by an initial five-year, $15 million investment, to align university resources, faculty expertise, and educational programs around six interconnected solution areas addressing humanity’s ultimate grand challenge.
Watch: Six Solutions for Humanity's Toughest Challenges
Shared Vision Our Infrastructure Our Advantage Get Involved
Faculty, staff, students, and partners working together on interdependent strategies to shape a more sustainable, secure, and resilient world
A faculty-driven task force identified six interlocking solution areas that now shape the framework for George Mason’s Grand Challenge Initiative . These solutions are rooted in the university’s core strengths and reflect its deeply collaborative, multidisciplinary approach to research, education, and community partnership.
One Grand Challenge, Six Bold Solutions
"George Mason is in the business of discovery. This means unleashing our bold ideas from their theoretical and laboratory boundaries, thoughtfully cultivating them as they take shape, and fearlessly deploying them as innovations that will transform our lives."
— Andre Marshall , program director, Strategic Partnerships Hub, National Science Foundation (NSF); former Vice President for Research, Innovation, and Economic Impact and President of the George Mason Research Foundation

Shared Vision, Cohesive Approach
Funded through an initial five-year investment of $15 million through FY30, the Grand Challenge Initiative will align university resources and a cohesive working culture around this shared vision to:
Enhance educational opportunities and integrate these solutions into the university’s degree programs.
Increase faculty talent and issue-expertise, including postdoc and graduate students.
Align current projects and seed new major research proposals through new pilots and grant programs.
Build infrastructure and resources such as labs, equipment, supplies, and training programs.
In partnership with the university’s billion-dollar campaign, MasonNOW , the Grand Challenge Initiative will work to secure partnerships, funding, and other support from government, industry, and nongovernmental organizations.
